[h3] As far as I can tell, this game is getting bombarded with unfair negative reviews from people suffering from a terrible affliction known as "Skill Issue." I'd like to leave a genuine review in spite of these poor unfortunate souls so readers can actually get a good idea of what they're buying. [/h3]  For context, I never played Slay the Spire 1, though I watched plenty of people play it. It always seemed like a cool concept to me, but I mostly play co-op games, so it wasn't something I expected to get invested in. When I heard Slay the Spire 2 had multiplayer, I was immediately interested. A friend gifted it to me, and we jumped right in.  After about 40 hours, I can confidently say this is a great game for what it is in [u]Early Access.[/u]  Having an RNG-based deckbuilder is something of a double-edged sword. Card games are already inherently random—you build your deck yourself, but once it's shuffled, you can't control what you draw (without cheating, of course). Adding another layer of RNG by having to build your deck from random rewards means every run becomes a game of "LET IT RIDE" with special relics or events that alter your deck flow.  [b]That's both good and bad.[/b]  On one hand, it encourages me to experiment with all sorts of different builds. On the other, I may only get to play my favorite build once every several runs because the game simply refuses to give me the cards I'm looking for.  [u]For example:[/u] > I play a lot of the Necrobinder. > I really enjoy the Doom archetype. > One run might hand me every Doom card I could possibly want, letting me build an almost perfect deck. > The next run might offer nothing but Soul or Otsy cards, with virtually no Doom support at all, forcing me into a build I don't really enjoy.  Once you've experienced all of a character's archetypes, you start recognizing pretty early whether a run is headed toward something you'll love or something you'd rather abandon because it simply isn't fun for you. I'm honestly not sure whether that adds to the replayability or takes away from it.  I also come from years of playing Yu-Gi-Oh! (back in the older days), where I never really minded running larger decks. I understand that the most optimal way to play most deckbuilders is to thin your deck until you consistently draw your strongest combos or assemble an infinite.  Personally, though, I don't really care for the "my deck is now eight cards and I instantly win every fight" style of gameplay.  Yes, discovering an overpowered combo is fun...  [i]...the first time.[/i]  But getting angry at the developers because they nerfed infinite loops seems a bit silly when those strategies completely undermine what Slay the Spire is trying to be. The point is adapting to what you're given, improvising with the cards you find, and making the best of each run—not assembling the exact same nuclear deck every single time.  If that's what you enjoy, more power to you. Just respect the developers if they don't want those strategies to be trivially easy to force every run. As far as I'm concerned, stumbling into an infinite should be a rare, exciting dopamine hit—not the expectation.  So far, I really haven't had any major complaints... except that I absolutely hate the Knowledge Demon, but I'm not about to leave a [strike]childish[/strike] negative review because one enemy bullied me.  My only real criticism is that some multiplayer enemies seem to have far too much health. Aeonglass, in particular, feels absurdly tanky considering what its passive does. My friend and I consistently struggle to even get it below half health, and on a good run we might push it to around 25% before Withering eventually wears us down. That's also the case with a lot of Elites, whereas in a solo run I always opt to grab the Stone Sword for killing 5 Elites.. I absolutely avoid it at all costs in multiplayer since those enemies REALLY slap hard due to the scaling.  I also think it'd be nice if there were some way to gently influence a character's build path. For example, if I'm playing Necrobinder and really want to pursue Doom, maybe I could mark it as a preferred archetype before the run. It shouldn't guarantee Doom cards, but perhaps it could slightly increase the odds of seeing them. Outside of expanding the existing characters or adding entirely new ones, that's probably my biggest wishlist item.  I'd also love to see some additional game modes. A Turbo Mode, for example, where a run is roughly half as long. Maybe you start with extra Energy, stronger cards, and more relics, but the enemies scale up dramatically to match. A normal hour-long run becoming a frantic 30-minute sprint could be a lot of fun.  And, of course...  [b] Please give us cosmetics. [/b]  I desperately want to put a tiny hat on Otsy.  ...Or Byrdpip, my beloved (also make him bigger when I upgrade the card or multiply him when I dupe it pretty please with a History Course ontop).  Overall, I absolutely recommend this game. If you enjoy roguelite deckbuilders and PvE co-op experiences, there's a lot to love in this'n. I sincerely hope the developers continue expanding it with more cards, characters, relics, events, and game modes.  Keep it up, y'all. You're doing a great job. :)  [h1]TL;DR 8/10 Absolutely a great title for some deckbuilding PvE fun with your friends, hope the devs keep up the great work[/h1]

If you are a casual fan of slay the spire or other roguelike deckbuilders, get this game. It's a great upgrade from the original that preserves the original's charm while building upon it with interesting changes, like ancients replacing boss chests, epochs revealing lore and new unlocks, and fun new events. If you enjoyed the first game, you'll probably enjoy this game too.  That being said, if you're a more extreme fan who enjoyed the unique difficulty of the first game, this game IS NOT FOR YOU. It's still in its early stages, so it's forgivable, but the balancing is atrocious at times. It's definitely a step down from the original. Some bosses are absolutely incomparable to one another. You're telling me the dumbass mordekaiser crab is supposed to be on the same level as the insatiable? In what universe? The crab stuns itself and hits high damage once every like 4 turns. The insatiable has upwards of 300 health, hits 30 damage every turn AND gives itself strength, while forcing you to waste energy on useless cards or you die instantly. It's ridiculous. Normal enemy combats aren't balanced either. If you play on ascension, you better hope and pray you get the underdocks instead of the overgrowth so you can avoid the dreaded flyconid + snapping jaxfruit encounter. It doesn't make sense that a supportive enemy should be able to apply multiple turn lasting debuffs that make it impossible to block anything, then attack for 20 damage with ANOTHER ENEMY in the encounter that also attacks each turn. Low hp in the hive? Hope you don't run into the hunter killer and his 20 dmg a turn with one of the most debilitating debuffs in the game or the 4 cockroach encounter that hits for 18 each turn and takes minimum of 3 hits to kill each one so you can't oneshot them. There's no way to play around these because they randomly exist in normal enemy combats instead of elite combats. The ascension modifiers feel mostly fine. I never beat all of them in the first game, but in this game they feel fine up until the last one. Having to fight two act 3 bosses in a row with no heal or shop or anything is ridiculous with how strong the act 3 bosses are in this game. The test subject lizard thing is crazy. I always found the awakened one to be the strongest act 3 boss in the first game so I don't really understand why it had to be buffed and transformed in this game. Having to fight it on top of another boss can be soul crushing.  In short, the game is wonderful for fans of deckbuilders or just the original slay the spire. Game is fun with awesome new additions and a neatly improved art style. Can be frustrating for more dedicated fans who enjoy playing the ascensions, it might be better to wait until the game is better balanced as it gets further into its lifetime.  also RIP heavy blade and doormaker lol

Sometimes you'll misclick something and have to save & quit so you can try it again.    My other complaint is that the game feels like a better graphics version of the first game but with worse gameplay due to the poor balance.  There's not a lot of new and innovative ideas, it's just a more poorly executed version of the exact same game.    Overall, my biggest suggestion is to add the ability to gain a mana at the end of each round.  Sometimes I get stuck with 3 mana going into round 3 and it feels like an impossible hill to climb.  Just not enough gas in the tank to block and attack with 3 mana.  Either the cards need to get cheaper (which many of them do) or we need a better way to gain spending ability.    Hope to see it improve and will check back in once a year or so to see if it does.

It’s subtle, but upon comparison to the original, the visuals have received a welcome upgrade. This game is still early access which means they can turn it around. But they seem to be suffering from their own success and the balance changes seem geared toward removing player agency more than actual balance. They're probably focusing more on their future board game than making actual gameplay toward decision-making for their player base.  And for a roguelike, that's unacceptable. Why is resting at a campfire 99% of the time the best option before a major fight? Why are the most obvious card picks so pigeonholed?  Let me elaborate on that point. The Underdocks is a great example. I'm encouraged because of the enemies here to turtle for 2/3 of the elites as taking terrible attacks just leads me to be punished. Skulking colony limits how much damage you can do per turn and Phantasmal Gardners get block whenever you attack them. So for Ironclad, you either turtle until you have scaling, or vuln set up; for silent, poison; for Defect, damage orbs; for Necrobinder, doom; and for Regent, colorless/strength scaling. This is easiest way in general because of the lack of energy generation and mostly done through skills which give you the added benefit of block.  These SAME strategies are punished so hard in Act 2. Decimillipede and Infested Prism (especially the new one) laugh at your attempts to build any of the above I just mentioned. Did Book of Stabbing in StS, or Gremlin Leader, or Slavers care if you built in a specific way to play? No, as long as you had a balanced deck to block and have offense, you weren't directly punished for building in a certain way.  And that's the crux of the issue with this. I get there are people that are mass downvoting because they're upset with Doormaker, or Aeonglass, or whatever the next iteration of enemies are. And maybe that criticism is unjustified. But for those that are genuinely complaining that they can't make choices? Where are the changes that reflect those comments? They seem to only care about steering the game to how THEY think is best and that's a major problem. Because there really has to be some compromise. Look at Acrobatics becoming Uncommon. Why would one of the best cards for player agency become HARDER to find because they felt it was too centralizing? It doesn't make it any less selected, it only makes it more painful when these choices don't show up and you're stuck in a mediocre run for 20 minutes until your weak deck inevitably fails.

I played 450 hours of STS1 and more on my phone (a lot more but it's not recorded). I absolutely love STS1 and I see a ton of potential in 2, which is why I feel so bad about leaving this review. It makes me wish for a 'neutral' review option, but that doesn't exist so here we are.  STS2 has a problem. It's small, it's sneaky, and realistically it also existed in Spire 1, but it wasn't bad enough to make me write a review for that game. Basically, since 1, STS2 has less floors, far more cards, and a lot more enemies that don't just punish certain strategies but basically completely kill you for using them. Now, these things all need to exist (minus the less floors bit, add one or two to each act and it would help a lot) but the balance was super delicate. You add a few cards, make the enemies a little more single-solution-specific and tougher, and now you've got a really frustrating game.  I have each character (minus Regent, because quite frankly I don't like him very much) at a10, I've gotten all characters on 1 to a20, so I would say I know at least a little bit what I'm doing. I feel at this point, unlike the first game, a lot of the time when I lose runs it basically comes down to one thing: RNG. Yes, sometimes I needed to take that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ aoe card for a specific fight (sow into exoskeletons in act 2 for example) or I needed to take another damage common to get through act 1, but with the card bloat, it is now very possible I'm walking into fights like Lagavulin Matriarch or Soul Fysh with no good answers into them. It is very possible I really if I needed a solution that scales was not offered one that works well into Aeonglass or something and now I just die because I wasn't offered the tools to win.   A lot of the bosses now have way more RNG mechanics in their fights, like Vantom (who I see as a parallel to slime boss from STS1) giving unremovable statuses, and less off turns. Or Soul Fysh, who basically says if you draw 2 or more Beckons on an attacking turn, you lose. Or the Insatiable, now having an energy tax and draw tax built in that you cannot ignore or you automatically lose, regardless if your deck would have the output otherwise. Or queen, basically saying if you weren't offered draw (which except for clad, feels much more rare in this game) you are at quite a high risk of losing, or taking a ton of damage due to bound card RNG. A lot of the enemies feel way too strong, like Hunter-Killer, if you have the wrong build. Or, to a lesser extent, the floating statue guys in act 3. Pretty much all of the hard hallways in Act 1 except for smoke guy and triple seaslugs, and I guess sometimes the inklets.  The ancient bonuses are way more varied, which on paper sounds good, and eventually it will be. Unfortunately right now it means I'm building decks with a bunch of random crap in case I see one ancient bonus act 2, for example I remove less strikes because soup, I need to add cards like afterimage or stone armor or p-strike in case I see clone, I need to add more 'generalist' stuff in case I see Prismatic Gem, I need to add lots of random cards in case of Yummy Cookie or Sandcastle, etc. Vaaku can sometimes brick, and a lot of runs with him it feels like I'm picking the least bad option. It makes me wonder why they removed the ability to skip the ancient relics, as we could skip boss relics in the first game. I think I'd almost never click it but it feels bad that the player choice to skip is now no longer present.  Basically, what I'm saying is, because there is less floors in the game, everything has been tuned up, and there's more cards, RNG plays way more of a factor in Spire 2 than I personally ever feel it did in 1. It feels less when I lose like "♥♥♥♥, guess I really did need to pick up card I didn't want for this specific fight', or 'guess I needed to avoid elites', and more like 'guess I needed a better ancient relic, or to just never fight anything ever until the boss and win with health.' Which I think is fundamentally flawed for a game like this.  The main fix to this in Spire 1 was shops. If you spent your gold wisely, because of the size of the card pool and all the other factors, you would always find something at least useful in a shop, but in this game, the relics are more expensive, you are more likely to brick a shop, and somehow they do just feel worse than in 1, in a lot of ways I can feel but I'm not sure I can articulate that makes them feel less like a bailout when your run is going bad, although they still serve that purpose but just not as well.  I also think the difficulty curve is kind of bad. This was also a problem in Spire 1, where basically Act 2 was the hardest by far, but in Spire 2 it's worse because Act 2 is still ridiculously difficult, but now Act 1 is even harder so scaling up for it is very difficult as well. And act 3 is kind of a cakewalk because 1 and 2 are such a gauntlet I rarely feel like I'm weak enough by 3 for it to be a challenge, as if I was going to be in that position, I probably lost by then. Act 1 needs to be a little easier, just things hitting for slightly less damage or something. Act 2 could probably do with being easier, I'm thinking in a very specific way though, like Hunter-Killer having a capped debuff stack that increases during the fight and Prism having less health (he has comparable health to act 1 bosses, what the heck is even that).

I wanted to give this game some time since it's Early Access, but the direction for the last few updates has been pretty clear, and I think the developers are, for some reason, intentionally creating the most boring and frustrating roguelike deckbuilder experience.   The crux of the problem for months now has been the third boss slot in Act 3. The Queen and the Test Subject are broadly fine. Test Subject in particular is a threatening final boss that can still be reasonably accounted for in both deckbuilding and your strategy within the fight. Queen is maybe a little easy, but not a complete pushover. The third boss, however, has been a complete train wreck since the start and they've made several attempts to change it, up to and including *deleting it and replacing it with a new boss,* and yet at no point during any of these stages was it a fun, rewarding fight. At first it was way too easy, as it effectively did nothing. Then they kept adding gimmicks until it was a bloated monstrosity that had 3 phases it cycled between every turn, each with a unique debilitating debuff that punished certain types of deck strategies. The main problem here was that many strategies were hard-countered by ALL 3 of the phases, making those strategies effectively not exist within the context of the game at all, and the card rewards that lean you towards that path were just "pick this to lose the game" options. This problem got so bad that they just deleted the boss.  So what'd they replace it with? A new one, Aeonglass, who did... absolutely nothing, just like its predecessor's first iteration. Just sat there throwing out attacks and getting hit, like it was a very large version of the floor 1 enemies. Obviously this couldn't continue, so they gave it a gimmick and buffed the ever-loving hell out of it. Now it's a massive HP wall that gains armor, nullifies debuffs, adds unplayable status cards to your hand every time you play X number of cards, and also has turns where it shuffles even more of them into your deck while increasing the damage that all of them do to you at the end of your turn if they're still in your hand. They managed to recreate the exact same problem as the previous boss immediately, and to an even greater degree. Doormaker (the previous iteration) was certainly annoying in its deckbuilding restrictions, but wasn't fundamentally that much harder than the other two bosses. For the last whole beta cycle and major patch, Aeonglass has both been incredibly oppressive towards deckbuilding on top of being astronomically stronger than the other two bosses. As a result, every single run from before you even set foot on floor 1, you are just thinking "how do I not immediately lose to Aeonglass." Every card reward, every relic, every event, every Ancient, all of the decisions you could be making throughout a run collapse into the singularity of Aeonglass insurance.   And the worst part is that some characters get punished far more than others by this gimmick, to the point that several sub-"archetypes" within classes, like Shivs on Silent, or Souls on Necrobinder, feel like they're completely unpickable from the start. Is the boss unbeatable? No. Should the final boss not require any deckbuilding consideration? Also no. But is the game fun when every decision you make through an entire 45min-1hr run is solely through the lens of: if I pick this, do I die to Aeonglass? Also no. Not even close.   The start of a run in a roguelike is supposed to be the most magical part. You're back to square 1 with the entire game's branching possibilities at your fingertips. Maybe this run, I'll end up with a wildly different strategy and loudout than the last one. Maybe this run, an ability that is otherwise not great will end up being key to my success because I was presented with a unique challenge that wasn't there in a previous run. Maybe I'll get some kind of ability or relic that breaks something and I can diverge off into a new path that's completely different from what I was planning on. Slay the Spire 2's boss design takes this magic, and smothers it to death with a pillow before it can even get off the ground. Before I even begin a run, I'm already sighing at the prospect of building "the Aeonglass deck" yet again. Card rewards, relic rewards, Ancient rewards, they all lose their excitability because there is a correct answer for every run, and if you're not given the correct answer, it sucks to suck.   This problem had already demotivated me from playing the game at all for this last month or so, and the new Beta branch update not only leaves Aeonglass as it is, but actually guts one of the few counters the fight had in one card on one particular class. As if the cardinal sin of Slay the Spire 2 is having a run where Aeonglass isn't the be-all end-all. Having finally beaten the game with all characters and having a ton of fun till this point, StS 2 deserves a very positive review from me.  TLDR: Like StS 1 an absolute recommendation.  [h3]If you have played StS 1 before[/h3] You will immediately recognize the game and feel at home, while still having a fresh experience. The three old characters have about half of their card pool renewed. The old formula of pathing is unchanged, events and enemies are completely new (although you will recognize some old movesets) and in terms of mechanics there are only little and careful additions. Though those mechanical additions are small, their impact is huge, as now there are even more ways to completely escalate your decks out of control.  In terms of difficulty I'd say it is, as of now, easier than the first part on maximal difficulty. But still by no means a walk through the park.  [h3]If you didn't play StS 1 before[/h3] StS 1 is a classic and I see no reason why the second part wouldn't achieve the same status regarding its current state. If you enjoy deckbuilding and don't shy away from a challenge, chances are, that you will enjoy this game. With a successful run averaging about roughly more than an hour (depending on your playstyle of course), the time investment for a session is acceptable for most people.  It is however not always easy and can even be frustrating to newcomers. Why is that? First, the randomness of this game. If you start a run and have a strategy in mind from the beginning, you are very likely to lose and get frustrated. This game wants you to adapt throughout the whole run and punishes bad choices fast! Second there is no real metaprogression. Initially you will unlock new cards, relics and potions. But, in contrast to similar games, those unlocks are not stronger, but just different options, that offer more variety to your runs. The real  progression happens in your brain, as you get a deeper understanding and are more reliably able to build ridiculous decks. Your only real option of progress is to make the game harder for you, not easier. Which I think is a good thing!

Everyone complaining about Aeonglass and Doormaker when Test Subject is still kicking my ass and somehow showing up to every multiplayer run.  While we mourn the loss of Doormaker, I'll provide something unexpected.  The only thing we're missing is a release of the soundtrack, which I look forward to. But so far, it's great. Every song deserves its own description of praise for how well it fits, with my personal favourites being Ceremonial Beast, Soul Fysh, Knowledge Demon, Waterfall Giant, and the Underdocks Area theme.  So, just for now, can we pour one out for Clark Aboud?  Overgrowth A - My personal preferred Overgrowth theme, I love the somewhat melancholy, curious tone.  Overgrowth B - Someone once described this as perfect for "Stalking through the jungle", couldn't have said it better myself.  Overgrowth Elite - Seems like a normal tough enemy theme, but then hits you with a phase 2, perfect introduction to elites.  Vantom - Really hits you with the dynamic music informing you that this is no ordinary boss battle.  The Kin - Helps set itself apart from Vantom by creating the sense that you're fighting a person instead.  Ceremonial Beast - My personal favourite theme in the entire game. Regal and reverent, The Ceremonial Beast itself practically doesn't belong next to the other monstrosities in the game, and that's in part thanks to this theme.  Underdocks - My favourite area theme, truly combining the sense of wonder and treacherous danger of the water.  Underdocks Elite - A step up from the Overgrowth Elites, which makes sense since you physically can't encounter the Underdocks in an early playthrough. It's almost bragging about being different to Overgrowth, in a way.  Waterfall Giant - Someone said the 5/4 rhythm "drives the piece forward", which is how I'd put it too. It really helps make the almost depressing tone of the piece feel even heavier when the main motif kicks in.  Soul Fysh - I loved this theme the moment I first heard it and realised Soul Fysh was getting a boss theme. It goes all in on the wonder of encountering something in the water, as if the boss really is hypnotizing you to your death.  Hive A - Hive always felt oddly gladiatorial, and this theme is why. It's basically saying "alright, you had your fun with the tutorial, now let's see how you handle this."  Hive B - I prefer this theme, however. It really feels like you're roaming in a den full of bugs and the clashing rhythms help bring that sense of creepy crawliness together.  Hive Elite - This one feels oddly personal, as if it's evoking the gladiatorial vibe of Hive A. Makes sense when you find out firsthand that the Hive Elites are a CONSIDERABLE step up from the Act 1 Elites.  The Insatiable - Yup, this is "Giant Worm is trying to eat you" music. Nailed it. Though a funny comment also said this is what it's like to see a deadline approaching. 10/10 description, pack it up.  Knowledge Demon - Like The Kin, this theme gives you the sense that you're fighting something more intelligent, but Knowledge Demon is far more intimidating and malicious, as if this seemingly ancient being has far more power than you could know.  Kaiser Crab - Somehow more monstrous than The Insatiable. This theme really gives the sense that you're not fighting this boss, you're *surviving* it. Amplified even more by the fact that the boss doesn't even die, it just retreats.  Glory A - Feels truly daunting in the intro, as if you're on your last legs, which you might be. But it becomes more determined and resolute later on, as if acknowledging that you actually are managing to make it far.  Glory B - Still has a sense of finality, but is more encouraging overall, as if to say "You made it, now go get 'em!". I definitely like hearing this theme when I have a silly ass deck that destroys everything in obscene fashion.  Glory Elite - Definitely tells you that you're fighting more powerful beings than ever before, which makes sense considering the lack of a distinct area theme in Act 3 besides technology, the mark of intelligent beings. You're in for some real foes now.  Queen - The climactic final boss theme, the light at the end of the tunnel, blocked only by one last foe. Queen definitely benefits from this boss theme the most, however, and that's thanks to the fact that what you first hear is only phase 1. Phase 2 becomes far more personal and that's why it took me a while to like this theme, it just really didn't fit the current placeholder act 3 bosses that aren't quite complete yet.  Test Subject - Oh Test Subject, I love you, I hate you, but I still love you, and then hate you some too. Incorporates the Act 3 boss motif very tastefully as the fight escalates from a solvable problem to something out of your hands very fast. I just feel it really sells the gravity of how prepared you must truly be to face Test Subject, even if it seems unassuming at first. "Pff, just another big monster, not even as big as the other ones I've face so far..." "...oh ♥♥♥♥."  Merchant - One of the only themes that evokes a sense of familiarity and warmth. It really helps you grow attached to the merchant and his enthusiastic voice. Sometimes I just spam click just because hearing his voice with the whimsical music makes me chuckle.

I wouldn't normally post an EA review this early, but the game is being review-bombed, so I'm weighing in.  Ultimately, this is a super-satisfying title. It feels both comfortable and challenging.   BALANCE & GAMEPLAY  The game needs some balance work. It can be super-frustrating to own the floor, only to get whomped by the final boss. The devs have nerfed the fun stuff a bit too much; infinites are cool, and game-breaking is half the fun.  However, the balance is actively being attended to, so I don't see it as an issue.   THE ROSTER  3 characters have returned so far: the Ironclad, Silent, and Defect. Each has been tweaked. The Silent's poison has been nerfed, but she is arguably more interesting for it.  Notably, the Watcher missed the cut. I think there's a reason for that.  There are 2 new characters: Regent and Necrobinder. The latter is quite playable and introduces some interesting defence-based mechanics. Regent, OTOH, feels like playing Microsoft Excel and will probably end up about as appreciated as the Watcher.   VERDICT (SUBJECT TO CHANGE)  Even without final art, achievements, and a complete storyline, this is a must-have game.  It just feels so good to be back in the spire again.  Highly recommended.

Review as of 29/6/26.  I have a10 on ironclad, defect, regent, a9 on necro, and a3 on defect (because I just can't CBF anymore).   Evaluating Slay the Spire 2 right now requires looking at it through two completely different lenses: what the game promises to be, and the chaotic reality of live game development.  The underlying issue hitting the Steam charts is that StS2 was released too early for the general public, despite being explicitly labeled as an Early Access title. Because of the massive pedigree of the first game, a massive wave of casual players bought in on day one. They didn't find a finished sequel; they found a true, unpolished BETA. For players expecting a complete experience, the missing endings and placeholder art make it feel like it was pushed out prematurely. Imagine if Silksong did this - absolute chaos. We have only two brand-new faces: the Regent and the Necrobinder. The remaining slots are filled by the exact same legacy characters we have already spent hundreds of hours mastering. While grinding the new classes.  This is most evidenced in the in the game's balance. Mega Crit is treating this period as a true testing ground, aggressively nerfing broken infinite combos and adjusting mechanics live. This has created a hostile review environment. Players who logged in during the first weeks and found fun, broken builds are now returning to find those builds completely gutted. The constant shifting goalposts make the grind exhausting. While pushing into the high single-digit Ascensions on the newer characters rewards experimentation, trying to play returning characters like the Defect highlights the balance disparity.   Ultimately, the community is committing a classic review sin: comparing a raw, developing prototype to the finalized, immaculate state of StS1. The original game benefits from years of post-launch stabilization. This sequel will either remain a polarizing, frustrating experience in its current "live-patched beta" state, or it will finally earn its praise when it reaches a definitive, finalized version 1.0 release. Until then, it is a playground for active testers, not a casual hobby.   For anyone on the fence about the game - yes, get it, its fun. But don't review. Everyone should stop reviewing. Frankly I think this is one of those instances where reviews literally do not reflect the game. I won't be playing until the game is in final - or when a new character is released.

I can say however, the graphical fidelity, overall animation fluidity, technical upgrades, and breadth of previously static encounters feel like a breath of fresh air. Where to start, this game is perfect for people who grew up playing Deck builders like DC deckbuilder, or Dungeons and Dragons, with a flare for the combat systems. It's well rounded, with fun to offer in many forms, as each run of the spire feels unique and randomised accordingly. The game has many improvements from the first, from it's animations and room design, to the bosses and difficulty of the game (I believe is a strong step up) but still presents a fun way to play.   The multiplayer aspect gives a new angle, allowing users lots of excitment with crazy builds and decks that one shot big bosses by the end, again the game's strongest attribute is that it doesn't shy away from giving you the chance to go ham with cool set ups. There's amazing cards and great mystery rooms, it's always a gamble to see where you're going to end up and if you'll survive.   Take time to read room descriptions, and look about the designs, there's often small easter eggs that previous players will appreaciate (have a look in the background of the final boss room).   An exceptional upgrade, although I personally miss the character "Watcher" i find the new characters are very awesome and bring their own unique twists to the game. I loved the original, and Slay the Spire 2 is such a massive improvement in so many ways: - MULTIPLAYER!!! It is so so much fun to play with friends, and they even have special cards that help your friends. It gets really interesting when you end up playing a particular role like tank or debuffer. My most unique role was to do a bunch of damage and die every combat and have my friends drag me to the next room. The tricky thing is that not everyone will have a good deck at the same time, so one person might be obliterating enemies while another is struggling.  - The UI and QoL are significantly better (e.g., the compendium being accessible during runs, thorough run history tracking, drawing on the map). - Events are more interesting, with few "do nothing" events like there were in StS1. - There's a greater focus on improving cards (e.g., enchantments, archaic tooth), making it feel more like a card game which is cool as hell. - An alternate act 1, which makes runs feel a lot more variable. Very much looking forward to alternative acts 2 and 3. - More characters!! I also like the Regent and the Necrobinder much more than the Watcher (though it still would be cool if she returned as long as she had more variety in build type). - Builds are much more fleshed out than in StS1. Things like 0 cost decks for the Defect or sly decks for the Silent felt less developed in the original than they do now. Even the change to inferno just shows how much the developers have learned. - More ability to multiclass! I think it's so fun to get other characters' cards working in your deck, and I look forward to the day I get a supermassive or arsenal in my shiv deck. - Better art! I didn't really notice that the art was lackluster in StS1, but the game is so pretty and dynamic now. I especially love the unique backgrounds for the shop and certain bosses. The early access launch date trailer looked sick as well, and I wonder if they would ever add animated cutscenes to the game. - Since it's currently in early access, it's very easy to leave feedback (assuming your country's censorship laws allow) with the F2 feature. And they listen to our feedback!   I just love this game so much, and as much as I love StS1, all the improvements here make it hard to go back.

I love both Sts 1 and 2 and Sts2 is everything you could hope for in a sequel, the same game at heart, but with more depth, mechanics and environments play in (and it's still in Beta as a type this!). The devs seem incredibly responsive to player feedback and I can't wait to see what future patches bring to the game.   tl;dr of the differences between 1 and 2: Events can lead to "enchantments" for cards (one per card) which in the right combination can make for some crazy effects. There's no artefact for the player anymore and there are less ways to stack permanent strength/dex/focus, with more emphasis on "buff this turn only and make the most of it" which I think makes for more interesting fights. There's an alternate act 1 and 2, which is defintely fun and changes the way you have to build your deck. There's a little bit if lore now (still in progress) and the new visuals, card art, backgrounds, boss music etc feel really cool.  Multiplayer!! It's great, it doesn't feel clunky at all, it doesn't feel perfectly balanced atm (but we're still in beta) but it's so much fun dragging your friends up the spire, with everyone arguing over who selfishly blocks instead of killing etc and endlessly drawing on the map.  PSA - There have been a slew of negatively reviews lately, please don't get discouraged by them. It seems like players were using the steam review to push for balance changes, with some bosses being especially frustrating. The hardest difficulty is meant to be hard! A9/10 do not mess about, but you can still play A0 and build insane decks and blast your way through the spire.   10/10 - would (and have) absolutely recommend, especially if you can't promise ~1hr at a time to a gaming session. Walk away at anytime, try a run as many times as you need to, learn at your own pace, play with your partner/friends and slowly climb the ascentions, it's a great time.

I def felt in the first game that some builds were just objectively better than others, and always felt myself falling into certain builds just because they were the only ones that felt viable at higher ascension levels. In 2, largely because of the greater card variety, there's so much more to play around with and in my experience so far no single build feels fundamentally better or worse than another.   the cons: It's hard for me to gauge the difficulty, since i don't have that many hours and was never really amazing at the first game despite playing the hell out of it, but i def feel like there's more BS than the first. Some elites are just run-killers for me, which sucks the fun out of good runs.   Like i mentioned, i love the new cards and added build diversity. That being said, the sheer amount of new stuff can make it difficult to make a proper build early on, i've had a few runs where i just get a bunch of pieces of different builds i cant really put together. My other big issue, and the one which concerns me most, is the lag spikes. I mainly play this game on my laptop, which isn't the most powerful device but can run a few heavy games, and experience regular lag spikes every hour or so. They're not horrible, but very noticeable and i don't really understand why they happen, since the game is relatively simple and i more than meet the requirements. I'm not an expert on pc parts, so i've attacked my specs for you to judge. I am worried about how this game will work on mobile once it goes over there, as the first one did.   overall, i recommend. Slay the Spire 2 somehow accomplishes the impossible: it takes one of the greatest roguelike deckbuilders ever made and makes me wonder how I ever lived without the sequel.  From the very first run, everything feels familiar yet dramatically improved. The core gameplay loop remains as addictively brilliant as ever—every card choice, relic pickup, and path decision feels meaningful—but the new characters, mechanics, and encounters inject fresh life into a formula that was already near perfection.  What truly stands out is the sheer depth of strategic possibilities. Every run feels unique, constantly presenting impossible choices that somehow become your favorite moments. The balance between luck and skill is masterfully tuned; when you win, it feels earned, and when you lose, you immediately want to dive back in and try a different approach.  The art, animations, and overall presentation are a massive step forward without sacrificing the charm and personality that made the original so memorable. Battles are more dynamic, enemies are more creative, and the soundtrack perfectly captures the tension of climbing the Spire one floor at a time.  Most sequels add content. Slay the Spire 2 elevates an entire genre. It respects everything fans loved about the original while confidently pushing the design forward in meaningful ways.  This isn't just a worthy sequel—it's a masterclass in game design. If you enjoy strategy games, roguelikes, deckbuilders, or simply games that respect your intelligence, Slay the Spire 2 is an absolute must-play.

Good game, a lot fresher and more interesting then its predecessor, there are lots of things I like, obviously, having put in around 100 hours at this point, but I've grown tired of it to the point I will probably be setting it aside rather than putting 100+ more hours in for a few reasons. As someone who almost exclusively plays rougelikes and has thousands of hours poured into them these are some things that would improve the game.   The multiplayer is one of the coolest and most unique things about this game. Getting my friends who don't play rougelikes to play a rougleike with me is not a day I ever thought I would see. However, the scaling of enemy stats and buffs/abilities for multiplayer need to be more fine tuned. To name a few instances where some enemies are exponentially more difficult in multiplayer, the Vantom boss starting off with like 99 stacks of slippery, the thieving hopper needing to be hit by 15 attacks to be knocked out of flight, and the Ovicopter's summons having more hp than the player (70-80).  Some of the Ascension modifiers make the game less fun, chiefly the one that makes rare cards appear less often. This wouldn't be as much of an issue if the card pools were larger but the result of this ascension modifier is runs are more boring because you see the same card choices in card rewards far more often. I normally love the challenge of ascension, and similar implements in other rougelikes. I've gone beyond heat level 20 in hades.   If the devs fix those 2 things then I will probably put at least 100 more hours into the game.  Some game mechanics single out 1 or 2 characters and are much more challenging to deal with when playing those characters to the point that sometimes if your deck isn't optimized against these specific mechanics, these encounters can easily end your run single handedly. The tender debuff from the hunter killer, the personal hive power on the entomancer, and the power of the aeonglass are all far more difficult to deal with when playing the silent or the defect (and less so, the regent), especially the entomancer for the silent. Builds where you play a lot of cards in a turn are extremely commonplace for these characters and are also some of the most fun decks to build, and to have enemies that counter those builds so severely that they can single handedly end runs is very frustrating. The most frustrating one by far is the aeonglass which was so disappointing for me since I had the same complaint about the timekeeper in slay the spire 1. Going through 2 acts just to see that you scored the 1/3 chance of a boss that you probably have no chance against because of your deck build is frustrating and discourages players from building a wider variety of decks. Sure, you can build decks for the silent or the defect which handle these encounters better but again, its not fun to feel restricted on what type of deck I can build by a singular enemy that I may or may not encounter. I think that there are good ways to counter certain playstyles while not punishing the player too harshly. A great example of this is the debuffs offered by the knowledge demon. If I'm playing a shiv deck with the silent or a power/0 cost attack deck on the defect I know I can absolutely not take the "you cannot play more than 3 cards per turn" debuff from the boss and have to take the 6 damage per turn instead, but that to me feels fun and challenging rather than punishing.   PS: Some of the recent changes are bad. The infested prism rework is a disaster. It is now harder than some bosses and extremely difficult to deal with for any character aside from the ironclad, really. Of course I already mentioned the aeonglass and all of my issues with it. I didn't necessarily love the doormaker because the fight could become very one sided very fast if you got some unlucky draws, but generally I did think it was a fun and challenging mechanic to deal with, probably the most interesting and mechanically complex boss in the entire game. I guess I understand that most players aren't as smart as me *pushes up glasses* All of the other recent changes are great, my favorites being the changes to neow. Keep up the good work!

My main gripe with this game is that it clearly wants you to synergize your deck, but at the same time it punishes you for doing so. Want to make a fun shiv deck? You better hope you won't meet the Entomancer, or else say goodbye to the 30 minutes you spent on this run. You have a bunch of Soul-generating cards and you were absolutely breezing through the floors? Uh-oh! You just encountered the new Infested Prism and now you are dead. You've finally made your power deck work? Oopsie, apparently the Devoted Sculptor knew about your build and has been waiting on you since Act 1.  Of course the average Redditor mid-wit will tell you you should be prepared for all encounters, but there's a big flaw in this strategy, and that is the fact that it's NOT FUN. "Man, adding those extra shivs to my build would really help against 99% of the encounters, but if I have to fight [enter hard-counter here] then I'm screwed. I better take [enter boring, safe card here] instead just in case. If that sounds fun to you, then more power to you. But to me that is not fun. Am I saying there shouldn't be any counters in the game? Not at all! But there's a big difference between a challenge and straight up unfairness. At the time of writing, the devs have failed to find a balance between challenging gameplay and fun. And that is such a shame, because I WANT to enjoy the game. I really do. I can see the enormous potential it has, but I feel like that potential hasn't been realized just yet.   I feel like the developers have simply forgotten that games are meant to be FUN rather than frustrating. I can just imagine them sitting around an Ikea table in some poorly lit, carpented office room trying to think of ways to drain all the fun out of their own game. Why? I have no idea. I bought Slay the Spire 2 expecting a sequel.  What I got instead was a complete restructuring of my brain chemistry.  There are games you play for a few hours. There are games you obsess over for a few weeks. Then there are games that quietly move into your head, redecorate the place, and begin charging rent. Slay the Spire 2 belongs firmly in that final category.  Before this game, I used to make decisions like a normal human being. I would look at a situation and think about practical outcomes. Now I evaluate every aspect of life through the lens of card synergy and long-term scaling.  Someone asks if I want to go out tonight?  What's the opportunity cost?  Could staying home provide better value over several turns?  Do I have enough energy?  Is this conversation a trap event?  The game has fundamentally altered how I perceive existence.  Every run feels like a tiny universe. Every card pick matters. Every relic changes the trajectory of reality itself. You start with a pathetic deck full of garbage and somehow, thirty minutes later, you've become an unstoppable engine capable of violating natural law through sheer strategic momentum.  And the thing is: it never gets old.  Every time I think I've figured it out, the game introduces some horrifying new interaction that makes me question everything I know. A card I ignored suddenly becomes the centerpiece of a winning run. A relic I thought was mediocre turns into a divine gift from the heavens. A boss I considered easy reminds me that arrogance is merely another debuff.  The balance between randomness and skill is absurdly good. The game constantly presents chaos, but it never feels unfair. When I lose, I don't think, "That was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥."  I think, "I am a fool. The signs were there. The Spire tried to teach me and I refused to listen."  Then I immediately start another run.  And another.  And another.  Hours become days. Days become weeks.  At some point I stopped playing Slay the Spire 2 and started living it.  The art is fantastic. The animations are satisfying. The new mechanics somehow expand the original formula without compromising what made it legendary in the first place. It feels like the developers understood exactly why people have spent thousands of hours in the original and then decided to weaponize that knowledge against the entire human population.  This game is dangerous.  Not because it's frustrating.  Not because it's difficult.  But because it's so unbelievably compelling that it creates a gravitational field around itself.  I sit down intending to play one run.  Suddenly it's 3:17 AM.  The birds are awake.  Civilization has advanced several centuries.  My family assumes I've disappeared.  And I'm still calculating whether removing a Strike was worth the gold expenditure on Floor 12.  Slay the Spire 2 isn't merely a game.  It's a lifestyle.  It's a philosophy.  It's a higher state of consciousness.  I have become incapable of looking at a deck of cards without mentally evaluating upgrade paths. I see probabilities in my sleep. I think in relic combinations. My dreams have map routes.  Would recommend.  10/10.  Please send help.  Actually don't.  I have another run to start.

There are more options across the board for every character than the first game had, more opportunities to experiment thanks to a few choice random events, more options to play the game and take on the Spire in whatever way you see fit.  The new characters feel fleshed out (except for Necrobinder, heheheh), the replacement of boss relics with The Ancients feels like a valid change, the pool of relics and cards have a good flow for encouraging a new run, etc.  It's in Early Access, there are going to be problems to buff and balance out. That's to be expected and it's okay for people to not see eye-to-eye with that balance right now. But I'd say STS2 does a very good job of reworking the combat system, implementing new features like enchantments, the better cross-color deck potential, and the addition of vanilla multiplayer. As the game is now, I believe it is a strict improvement over the first... even if some of the bosses and enemy encounters feel more frustrating than empowering to defeat.   I'd give STS2 a 9/10; I'm 109 hours into the game and I have no intention of stopping now!

Get better, git gud, whatever. It's not fun for me. I would uninstall if it wasn't such a different experience in multi-player, where we can cover each other with MP cards, overlapping status effects, and even give each other block.   If you intend to play this only MP or, perhaps, if you only ever intend to play it SP, then I can give it a thumbs up. In the former, the game feels fun and dynamic. In the latter, you won't know how much more fun it is, so you can repeatedly die without feeling the elation of easy(er) victories.  Make no mistake, MP isn't [i]easy[/i], per se. It's just far less frustrating. We can see how we lost. We can see how the RNG failed us in such a long string that it wasn't recoverable and neither of us could carry the other. SP punishes mistakes and RNG brutally. And I'm just not having fun. Thumbs down.

One of the biggest complaints you will here about this game is its difficulty. While I cannot say that this is an easy game in any sense of the word, I find the complaints to be a little ridiculous. Will this game challenge you? Yes. Will you lose way more runs than you win in the beginning? Absolutely. Will you invest an hour into a run, create a sick build, and then get hit with the perfect counter and lose the run? Frequently.   But there in lies the fun of a roguelike game. This game seriously rewards you for trying, failing, trying, failing, and repeating. There is so much strategy that goes into this game, and even 110 hours in for a game that is in early access, I still find myself enjoying the and learning every step of the way. I probably lost 20 games before finally beating Act 3, but holy cow did it feel so amazing when after hours of feeling like I was making no progress, I finally not only succeeded, but discovered a pattern of successes as I became more comfortable with the game. In my opinion, this is the epitome of what makes a roguelike game fun. You run in like a chicken with your head cut off, get destroyed, unlock some new items or mechanics, and then go back in having learned something and being able to improve your skills. I especially appreciate that I barely even looked at any guides online. I think I watched one video with some tips, and then was able to blaze my own trail from there.  If you are looking for an easy game that will hold your hand or let you win, this is surely not the game for you. But if you are someone who finds thrill in the passion of developing new skills, or the payoff when you finally achieve a goal you have been working towards, then this game is an absolute must buy.  I am so pumped for more content to come out for this game. It already feels so complete and well rounded. I can't wait to see what is coming next, because so far I have massively enjoyed playing the public beta and seeing the new additions as they come out.

StS2 is a game I got a decent amount of enjoyment out of. I was a big fan of StS1, and StS2 hit a lot of the same notes for me, at least for a while. However, it has numerous issues that make it feel like a worse game than StS1 and stop me from recommending it.  First and most obvious: the game is barely a sequel and more of an expansion pack. The amount of new content is extremely sparse. There's only two new characters, neither of which are as well-designed as the originals. There's new enemies, but most of them just feel like infinitely-scaling damage sponges, while the rest just have a mechanic that completely counters some strategies while being a non-factor for all others. There's a multiplayer mode, but that has its own host of issues. For anyone who wants a game that is an evolution of StS1, or fixes issues they might have had with it, definitely skip this one.  Another issue, and the one that compelled me to write this review: the updates. The most obvious example is everything involving the Doormaker. It wasn't a particularly compelling boss before, but Mega Crit have made it clear that they have no idea what they're doing with this boss. They kept making changes, each more drastic and less thought out than the last, giving it mechanics that just completely nullify strategies that are otherwise good against basically everything else. Then they just removed it completely, claiming it was too complex. 1. This wasn't an issue people were complaining about, making it seem like they just completely failed to understand what their players were actually saying. 2. This is an indirect insult towards the people upset with the boss and stokes division among the playerbase by adding fuel to the claims that all the complainers were just too stupid to beat the boss (they weren't). 3. The boss wasn't particularly complex or difficult to understand. This idea that a boss having more than two mechanics is too complex is just baffling. This is just the most extreme example of nonsensical balancing the game has received, but the fact remains that none of the updates have made the game better, and some have made it worse. I've seen people say that the devs aren't listening to players, and others say that they're babying the loudest parts of the playerbase, but I think the core issue is more depressing: they're [i]trying[/i] to listen to the players, but they're just [i]really bad[/i] at it.  The game STRONGLY favors offensive strategies over defensive ones, largely because so many enemies hit ridiculously hard, scale as the fight progresses, or both. Unless your strategy can immediately turn defense into explosive offense, building around anything other than immediate explosive damage will quickly get your HP worn down, either because the enemies scaled as you tried to stall them out, or you got unlucky and drew your attack cards on a turn where the enemy did a ton of damage.  The multiplayer is the big new feature the game has. Really, it's the [i]only[/i] new feature the game has. Unfortunately, this feature has a host of problems that have stopped me from investing more time into it. The biggest one is the need to climb a separate ascension ladder from single player. I've gotten up to A10 with multiple characters, yet I have to start from A0 when playing multiplayer. This makes getting into a high-ascension game WAY more tedious than it needs to be, since [i]every player[/i] needs to be at that level. Another issue is that it kinda just feels like 2-4 people playing the same single player run at the same time, rather than a cooperative experience. There's a few co-op exclusive cards, but they rarely provide the kind of synergy that makes for satisfying moments with friends. Maybe that changes at higher ascension levels, but again, dragging people up through lower ascensions is too tedious for me to bother with.  A relatively minor nitpick, but the aesthetic and writing of the game are mediocre at best. They added a bunch of lore bits to the game, but they're so dull that I couldn't be bothered to read more than a few of them. The designs and visuals are functional, but nothing more. The original game didn't have amazing visuals/writing either, and neither of these things are really the focus of the game, but I figured it was at least worth mentioning.  Again, I can't really say this is a [i]bad[/i] game. It's just not a game I can recommend, knowing the amount of nonsense and mediocrity that comes with it.

As a sequel, this game succeeds most with its two biggest additions: the new playable characters and multiplayer. The fresh characters introduce exciting mechanics and deck-building possibilities, while multiplayer adds a completely new way to experience the game's strategic depth with friends. The presentation has also seen a noticeable improvement. The art style remains colorful and cartoonish, but characters and monsters are more detailed, animations are smoother, and the overall visual experience feels more polished and alive than the original. That said, the game can sometimes feel very familiar to veterans of the first title. Many cards and relics function almost identically to their original counterparts, and the returning characters feature fewer new cards than some players might have hoped for. However, there are still enough new cards, enemies, bosses, and mechanics to create fresh strategies and encourage experimentation. The redesigned boss relic system is particularly successful, significantly changing decision-making and making runs feel distinct from the original game. Since the game is still in early access, there is also plenty of room for additional content and features in the future. For newcomers, none of these comparisons matter much. This remains an outstanding deck-building roguelike and one of the strongest games in the genre. Whether you're a returning fan or discovering the series for the first time, it offers deep strategy, endless replayability, and a gameplay loop that is difficult to put down.

It’s absolutely baffling how unfinished this game feels. The design clearly pushes you towards bloated decks while actively punishing smaller ones, and the mechanics and balance are just fundamentally flawed. I’ve already cleared A10 with every character and even attempted some win streaks, but I’m completely burnt out on SL just to brute-force a run. The enemy design is a nightmare: some foes demand high single-hit damage just to break their guard or end the fight quickly, while others require a multitude of low-damage hits to take down. Trying to cram both into a single deck inevitably forces it to become massive. ST1 felt much more organic—you’d actually use the cards you were dealt and find creative ways to win on the fly. This sequel, however, feels like you’re building a hyper-specific deck from the very start just to counter a particular monster or mechanic. What used to be a thrilling challenge has devolved into a tedious puzzle to solve. Between the endless save-scumming and the soul-crushing RNG when you get a rubbish draw order, it’s honestly more frustrating than fun.

Slay the Spire 2 is a rogue like tower climbing card game which improves on every mechanic from the first game. Many encounters now include enemy scaling which discourages pure stalling tactics. New cards, keywords, and characters all meaningfully affect the gameplay experience and how you play the game. The way ancients are used as a way to reward the player for reaching the next floor make Neow and the other ancients feel impactful, acting as points in a run where you are not completely at the mercy of RNG.  Infinites are now much more difficult to accomplish than when the game first released, making the second game more in line with the first. Although ascensions only go up to 10, each ascension meaningfully impacts the run and ascensions 8 and 9 noticeably spike the difficulty. Ascension 10 is incredibly difficult, but doesn't feel outright impossible like higher ascensions (at least for me) felt like in the first game.  If you played and liked the first game, pick this up. Trust me, it's fantastic. If you haven't played the first game and are unsure about the second, don't worry. Playing the first game is not a prerequisite for playing the second and aside from one character that was not brought back, there is nothing that you will miss out on by playing only this.  All of that praise doesn't even include the awesome multiplayer functionality introduced here, which allows you to play with up to 3 friends at the same time and even introduces multiplayer only cards to spice up the experience. Please do yourself a favor and pick this up. On sale it's a steal but even at full price Slay the Spire 2 is well worth the price and I would highly recommend it.

In its current status the game is simply not fun in my opinion, for two primary reasons:   1. The primary pathing strategy involves actively avoiding combat encounters after the third combat in act I, and second combat in acts II and III, since they are pulled from a harder pool of enemies. These combat encounters are often harder than elites and offer poor rewards. It makes no sense that in a card game about fighting monsters, avoiding the core gameplay (the combat) is necessary to win.   2. The devs are trying too hard to design elites and bosses that can counter specific strategies: multiple enemies create status cards, which counter thin decks; there are enemies that punish playing skills, enemies that punish playing multi-hit attacks and enemies that punish playing too many cards per turn. And most of them scale very quickly. As a consequence of these design decisions, in order to maximize win rates, the player must draft a deck to kill enemies in as few turns as possible. Again, it makes no sense to me that in a card game about fighting monsters, the player must actively avoid engaging with the mechanics and strategy of the fight, by killing them as quickly as possible.  Due to these two fundamental issues with the gameplay, I cannot possibly recommend the game in its current stage. I will revisit it if these issues are ever addressed.

I feel that the constant anti-stalling precautions put in place of this game unnecessarily ruin builds and player expression for an issue that should be entirely within the player's control. YOU control the buttons you press, no one is forcing you to choose the 18+ hour long meta stalling deck nor is it required to win, and you shouldn't be forced out of it if you want to.  I never had an issue with this in Slay the Spire 1, I played and won Silent runs just fine without Wraith form, all the way to Ascension 20. My playstyle hasn't changed in Slay the Spire 2, and yet the "anti-stalling precautions" are now affecting ME with how almost every enemy gets strength now if you don't kill it fast enough. No I am NOT "setting up for an infinite" Mega Crit, I just don't kill every enemy turn 1-2!!  Fear of a boring meta is somewhat ruining this PRIMARILY SINGLEPLAYER game for me. So many other successful Roguelikes just don't do this because player fun is simply subjective and should be in the hands of the player, not mandated by the developers. Developers should offer the tools and challenges to do so, without intentionally crippling playstyles. And for, like, what? fear of players having impossibly high leaderboard scores no one will care for? Because that's what makes the game fun? That's what should have priority?  Oh and it doesn't even work!! I have still made infinite defend runs with Necrobinder! It purely exists to hurt my runs that just don't get a good early damage! Whether I have fun or not purely depends if I gamble that good Act 1 luck, since the higher healthpools of Acts 2 and 3 just mean they hit harder ON TOP of having more turns to hit me if my damage hasn't increased enough to kill them in ~2 turns yet ANYWAYS. It's a rogue-like sure, luck is like all over the genre, but having a chance at winning shouldn't feel "lucky". It should be the other way around, where losing feels unlucky.  Overall, the game fundamentally is good, however the idea that player fun is heightened by practically forcing a risky playstyle in order to win, is in my opinion flawed. Almost every enemy in the game scales over time, and it's just exhausting. Meta prevention should not be a prioritized concern like this for a primarily singleplayer game. Let players play however they want, NOT how the developers want. Nobody is forcing every player to use the current community defined meta strategy of "stick all you fingers up your butt for 10 hours straight", and if they think they need to in order to win that should be on them.

After finishing work every day, I just want to relax and enjoy a game — to have fun building my deck, exploring options, and feeling the satisfaction of overcoming challenges. I do not want to close the game feeling irritated and exhausted because the game kept punishing me over and over.  A game can be difficult. A game can be challenging. But it should still make the player feel like they are learning, improving, and getting stronger. Right now, it feels less like I am playing the game, and more like the game is playing me.  I sincerely hope the developers take another serious look at the current balance, progression, and sources of frustration. Please do not mistake unfair or unfriendly design for a “hardcore” experience.

I absolutely understand that it is in early-access, but the core design philosophy just leaves me feeling very unsatisfied.   It essentially amounts to punishing the player for having the wrong build. There are so many enemies that just hard-counter certain decks, and if you build around them, there are so many enemies that require the exact opposite deck. Experimentation is punished because you're never going to win without a tried-and-true method, except accidentally. Defensive builds are punished because basically everything requires a hyper-aggressive playstyle to keep from being overwhelmed. Flexibility is punished because outside of a few rare cases, the more cards you have, the more RNG is going to completely screw you over due to the aforementioned hyper-aggressive requirement.   Every winning deck feels almost exactly the same to me to play, even between characters, largely amounting to 'Now I'm playing every single card in my hand without thought, oh and sometimes I throw a potion'- Which was fun the first few times, and not very fun past that. It was a feeling I *never* had with 1, which encouraged you endlessly to try out different things.   2 wants you to play a very specific way and is built from the ground up to force you to play that way, which is antithetical to Roguelikes and Deckbuilders alike, which is why this is a negative review. Unless they completely pivot away from that mentality, it's not really something that early access can fix.

Started out ok with the unlocks but slows down after a dozen wins. That kind of progression is expected with roguelites but there's too little here and the quality is just not there. I can't recommend it as it is but I hope with more time (and maybe mods) I can change this to a positive review. It is in early access and the developers have a chance to really put things back on track by fleshing out the space for build diversity and reducing how front-loaded the fights and unlocks are. Right now it feels like the roguelike mode for Hearthstone.  My chief complaint has to do with the regent (one of the new characters) being entirely unwieldy and ass-backwards for a game like this. Half the stuff you try with him doesn't land because the game rewards big first turns and his thing is all about building up and transforming your deck. Didn't draw your combo starter? Oops! All the other characters at least give you options for quick plays, delays or fast card draw, but the regent is just slow.  He's even slower than the ironclad. This glacial pacing in a genre with so much RNG is just anti-fun; let the regent draw more cards at a price or actually do something consistent with his secondary resource pool. I found myself playing all the old characters well because they have more or less kept their individual strengths but the regent feels like a bad mod character that wasn't balanced for anything. The other new character plays well (and has easier mechanics for drawing cards quickly and delaying damage) but definitely has a learning curve if you've not played some of StS 1's mods with similar characters. There's better integration between the characters of Downfall and StS 1 than the original characters in StS 2.  I am still in low ascension ranks and felt like the bosses were so overtuned and the devs love giving them these big effects that don't leave room for strategy. Some turns, you just don't do much because enemy mobs can disable you quickly and without room for counterplay. The developers are saying they want to remove this stuff (I think they mentioned the doormaker boss as an offender?) but I can only review the game as I played it. Why is the doormaker even in the game? There's earlier bosses (demon of knowledge) and elites (praying mantis thing) that hurt harder than the end-game bosses because they just have too much of an effect that you can't counter and might break your build entirely.  Am I supposed to build the deck properly an act before I meet the boss? How do I know what elites I'm fighting? Some bosses don't have any counterplay at all; the steam boss blows up at the end of the fight and has a damage value for that attack that you cannot decrease in anyway except by ending the fight sooner. This means if you are unlucky and end the fight on a turn where you don't have any block cards, you're mostly just going to die. How do you fight against this? Just kill the boss as fast as possible, which is what you are doing anyway, making this a non-mechanic and simply a DPS check. So many bosses and elites follow this pattern to end up being DPS checks determined by how good your first hand is.  I wish they built somewhat more RNG-resilient mechanics that make playing your hand correctly more important than drawing the right cards. You can still mill and trim your deck at the various events and the shop but it doesn't feel like it's enough. The newer characters just expose this flaw more clearly than the old ones (and I have the benefit of years of experience with the old mechanics) but I hoped this game would be an evolution and refinement of the previous entry rather than an expansion. It just feels like a mod. Some of the relics also feel wildly out of balance with the rest; everything needs to fit together better if this game is going to be any good. So many cards would be better off having their rarity reduced and being more available in general; right now it's hard to get anything going in the deck building phase and harder to draw it at the right time.  I don't really understand the story, or even the reason for the inclusion of story cards, as the characters don't say much and the plot as explained in the cards seems rather stupid and all of it seems to have happened in the past anyway. I don't care about the characters, because they don't say or tell you much.   At the end of every run your character groans or says a dumb one liner and adds your deck value to a global counter before getting sent back down, like in StS1; who thought this needed a story should've integrated it more into the actual game.. The game has cool looking side characters and animations/art but you see all of them a million times with very little changing, because they just give you cards or relics and send you on your way. They don't give you quests or share anything insightful, but they sometimes drop hints about the world or your character. They are about as impactful as an extra reward screen at the end of every act, because that is how function mechanically and do nothing else. Is there something missing here?  A minor note: At the time of writing this, there seems to be a lot of reviews mentioning the work of a specific consultant on this game, but I haven't felt like this game even warrants that kind of consulting being done. There's barely a plot and none of the characters say much. The mentioned story cards only have a couple of lines of text, and all of the story related text put together cannot be more than several pages of 12 point text in a regular font. Someone reviewed this stuff and got paid for it? What?

If you don't get those juicy pulls, winning is next to impossible. Some people like that, and that's OK. I am not one of those people.  If I were to sum it up in one sentence: "STS1 requires you to build a cohesive deck and play your hands well to win, but STS2 requires that and a ♥♥♥♥ ton of luck on top".

Honestly, it's more of Slay the Spire 1, but overall just kind of better. It's still finding its footing with getting all the balance right around the new additions (hence the early access, reminds me a lot of StS1 early access), and there are some pain points, but overall it's an improvement in almost every way.  1. Better presentation - the visuals and sound design are just overall better with more animations and cleaner UI readability. Plus the Defect got one hell of a glowup.  2. Build diversity.  I felt like, personally, in StS1 each character had like 2-3 real "builds" that worked and you kind of had to quickly and rigidly slip into one of them as fast as possible, leading to it starting to feel stale after awhile.  So far it feels like StS2 has more paths to victory, though a bit less clear cut.  3. Path diversity.  StS1 was pretty much "You do as many elites as possible, no other thoughts needed."  Elites have been devalued a little bit in StS2, making some routing decisions feel more impactful and interesting.  4. Built in Multiplayer Co-Op without mods.  It probably needs some balance tweaking still, but it feels really fun to play with friends and make some really silly combos off each other.  Would like to see more multiplayer only cards added as well.  All in all, a great improvement to the formula and wonderful progression to the game.  And, I'll address the elephant in the room - people were loving and glazing this game no problem left and right until they saw a certain name in the credits and then started freaking out.
