My goal with this review is to be the most useful guide for if you should buy this game or not. I will divide this review into sections each one for a different group of player.  Who Should Not Play This Game: Let's start with who this game is not for. If you are the kind of player that wants a fast pace action game, a story-based experience or a competitive multiplayer game, don't buy this game. You will probably open it play it once maybe have a bit of fun but it won't be for you.  New To The Roguelike Genre: I think this game is at least worth a try. The roguelike genre is a punishing one because if you die you will have to reset and this game is no different. Your first runs will be difficult and you might die often but unlike most games in the genre, this will not be due to lack of technical skill. There is no twitchy reactions or anything of that sorts, this game is purely decision making. If you don't enjoy thinking thoroughly and making difficult decisions, this game might not appeal to you.   New To Card Games: If you are looking to get into card games, this game is perfect for you. Unlike some real life card games, you won't have to buy any packs or anything like that. The cards are also remarkably easy to read and understand. All of the mechanics in the game are super clear and pretty much everything has a tooltip that let's you see what it does. Another bonus is you don't need anyone else to play with you.  Fan of The First Game: If you liked the first game, then you most likely already bought this but just in case you are still somehow on the fence, buy it. This game improves on almost everything from the first game. There are more characters, more variation, multiplayer and much more. If you are concerned with balancing and whether the gameplay matches that of the original, there are better reviews of this game for that. My take is that while this game is a little bit easier than the first one, I like the overall experience of this one better because of the variety and new decisions you can make. This is also probably the cheapest the game will be ever be in early access, so just buy it.  People Afraid of Early Access Games: I completely understand being wary of buying a game that is not finished but if this is the thing that is holding you back, then I can soothe your concerns and tell you that this is probably the most polished early access game I've ever played. In fact, if tomorrow the devs announced that they will stop working on the game, the price tag is still worth it. The other concern is the changes that the game will experience. If you are the kind of gamer that hates when the meta changes and feels anger when a dev changes something in your game, then yeah you should probably wait for the game to be finished. Personally I love the biweekly updates to the Beta branch and seeing the game develop but I can understand wanting a more consistent experience.  People Who Want A Game To Play With Their Friends: This game does have multiplayer but this you really need to consider whether all your friends will be into. The game is not your mindless fun like many co-op experiences and good communication is key to enjoying the multiplayer. If you are looking for more of a party experience, you should look elsewhere. I also don't recommend you buying this game only for the multiplayer. While the multiplayer is great, it's more of a great bonus rather than the main package. Maybe wait for a sale if you want multiplayer only.

A fine game. Game mechanics are very similar to StS 1 but there's a huge amount of new stuff. All the locations, monsters, bosses, and events are completely new with nothing repeated from the first game. There are also two fun new characters. For the returning characters, about half of the cards are new and half are the old favourites (e.g. Defect still gets Creative AI). Relics, potions, and curses are a mix of old and new as well, but the general vibe is more stuff and more on the new side of the ledger.  The big selling point of StS 2 for me is proper cross platform online multiplayer. One player hosts, up to three others join, and the difficulty scales appropriately. There are also multiplayer specific cards for each character as well as multiplayer colourless cards. The only caveat with the multiplayer is that you need to be on the same game branch and the same game version for it to work, otherwise it just silently times out without explaining what went wrong. For best results get everyone on the beta branch and updated to the latest version.  Difficultly wise it's a bit similar to the Hollow Knight / Silksong situation in that this is a tougher sequel aimed at the hardcore fans of the first game. There are some settings you can use to tailor the difficulty, but if it's too much you can just stick to a lower ascension and you won't miss any of the game content. The only thing unique to higher difficulties are particular curses.  Start with StS 1 if you're new to it, but if you enjoyed the first one you can buy with confidence.

It's a genre defining game and the sequel just got everything right.

Slay the Spire 2 improves on the first game while significantly upping the difficulty. Expect for it to take a while to beat the game, but that doesn't mean it's boring along the way. Like many other roguelikes, you get the satisfaction of progressing further and further on each run as you slowly unlock more pieces you can encounter next time.   Being able to play co-op is probably the biggest selling point of this sequel compared to the first one, and the new characters are a nice complement to that. It feels like the Regent and Necrobinder were designed to support certain mechanics in the original three character's repertoires (i.e. Necrobinder's doom pairs very well with Silent's poison).   This game is also significantly harder. Depending on how you like to play, that either makes this game more or less appealing than the first one. For me, I like having the option to play the first one for a more casual experience vs. the second one for more of a challenge.  My main complaint is that sometimes the Act 3 bosses feel out-of-pace with the difficulty of the rest of the run. You can be steamrolling the whole time, and then the Act 3 boss can just stop your run like a brick wall. That can be a little bit demoralizing when it happens on your 1 hour+ co-op run multiple times. But that is sort of just the nature of these roguelike, dungeon-clear games.

Overall, if you enjoyed StS1, you will also enjoy this. They kept the whimsy, the satisfying combinations, the enjoyable random events, and they even made it clearer what to do for unlocks. The art is lovely and they've expanded the story. I strongly recommend the game- especially for the multiplayer. It may not be perfectly balanced but multiplayer is extremely fun.  On a more technical note, I appreciate the devs are willing to continue design decisions to make the game harder and continuing to try to keep difficult fights despite getting pushback. For a while, I originally thought this game was harder than Slay the Spire I. The enemies feel like they scale faster and like block is more critical.   However, the more I play it the more I think that's not the case. Once you get a feel for good builds and a balanced attack/defense strategy, with knowledge what's in the game it's easier to force your way through regardless of the enemy. StS1 was a little less forgiving with their enemy strategies, but I think they're little by little working more of the difficulty into StS2. I'm enjoying their work and additions so far and look forward to where they're taking this game.

I debated for a while whether I should write this review for the game as it is, or as I believe it will be once it leaves early access. And I decided that I would write a review for the game as it is today, even if it changes in three months, because trying to predict the future never pans out.  I enjoy the game and I think it's good, but there are still a lot of rough edges. Enemy identity is fuzzier than in the previous game because almost all enemies follow the same set of mechanics. Spike damage to test your defenses, a turn for a debuff or card dilution, and strength growth in cycles. There are exceptions and cool ideas especially in act 2, like an enemy that will permanently steal cards, but in general fights feel more same-y. While it does mean the difficulty is less spiky (resulting in more consistent wins), it also makes most battles pretty forgettable because most of them play out the same. Also, once you realize that each character is built around a specific mechanic almost unique to that character, even decks that supposedly would have very different archetypes end up using 70% of the same cards and the same overall strategies. I got bored of the game well before I hit the 100-hour mark but I couldn't articulate why until recently.   Now that all sounds quite bad, but I do still recommend it because the basic deckbuilding fun of the first game is still here, the multiplayer is actually very nicely handled, and given the success of the first game we can assume the devs know what they're doing and the rough edges will probably be patched out.

There is something to be considered regarding releasing a game this unfinished in its production and the overuse and overreliance of 'Early Access' in the gaming industry to release and sell unfinished or unpolished products to the public, but personally I still enjoy this and am glad that I get to be a part of it.  Last thing to note is that it got review bombed a while ago mainly by international audiences because of certain balance changes, which are going to be frequent. The balance changes, I mean, I don't know about the review bombing. But hey, they like the game and they cared enough about it to vie for a change they wanted. Amending my review to a thumbs up because, while I mostly still agree with my review below, I think I had a misunderstanding of how beatable Act 3 bosses actually are. Leaving my initial thoughts for the dev's consideration, but I don't see it as negative enough to give this otherwise fantastic game a thumbs down.  Original Review:  This game has incredible potential, enough to be an all-time favorite for me. However, its current state is significantly marred by Act 3's boss fights, which you will see echoed across other negative reviews and for good reason. The bosses are overly restrictive and feel fundamentally unbalanced.  The difficulty of the bosses feel... mostly fine. The problem exists in their design. The mechanics currently force players to abandon fun or optimized deck-building from Acts 1 and 2 simply to survive one specific boss fight. This creates a whiplash effect. I build up anticipation, only for the effort to feel useless if the final act dictates such narrow solutions.  The difficulty curve is inconsistent. I can easily clear Act 3's intermediate floors, but the final boss feels disproportionately designed, making even a victory feel unearned and tedious.  While the core gameplay loop up through Act 2 is phenomenal, this single bottleneck severely degrades the experience for me. I'm changing my previous positive review to negative in hopes the devs will notice the shared sentiment from the player base and find a resolution without compromising difficulty. It’s a shame because the game has so much good content and is positioned to be a phenomenal follow-up to the first game. Here's to hoping!

Game is good. If you do not like to lose, this is NOT the game for you. Some of the balancing on hard-mode non-elite fights needs to be fixed (looking at you hunter).   Stability on the game is very good for EA. I've crashed maybe 3 times total.   Balance A8 and below are fantastic and you SHOULD be able to beat it with some work learning interactions and proper planning (Elite fights are your friends). A9 and A10 are rough and can be a little bit heavy on the RNG side.   Multiplayer balance -  2 player is very unforgiving. I would argue its harder than single player. This is just a number tweak. Less stacks of artifact and less health gain on enemies would make a world of difference. 4 player - Very fun and can be very broken.  3 player - Solid. Slightly easier than single player. Allows a newer/weaker player get carried a little bit.    Characters and design  IronClad - Full offense is the strat. Sometimes defense works out but its rare.  Silent- Very solid all rounder but does get countered pretty hard by the new Aeonglass boss. This character could really use a bludgeon-esque card to build around.   Defect - You want to play his gimmick (orbs) but generally a beat down deck will do better as orb cards can get droughts Necrobinder - THE defensive character. The allotment of cards the necro has is fantastic and legitimately has multiple angles archetypes.  Argent - Solid character. Builds really heavily support kingly or star builds. Making a heavy forge deck really feels like a bait.   Overall for EA this is fantastic. The are still a dozen or two cards that could use some tweaks and the hard pool fights could use some balancing tweaks. Rewards from normal fights may need some improvements as events are VERY strong.

I unfortunately can't recommend the game in it's current EA form. But hey, it's EA, and they have plenty of time to work out the balance. Stability wise, the game is great in both single and multiplayer forms. Upgraded art styles from the first game is very nice, and more seem-less animations help it look even better. It's a lot more pretty. Unfortunately, as a RL, the replayability mileage may vary.   The deck building can be varied and awful. The game wants you to be working with what you get, but not all base decks work well with each strategy, and there are not enough removal options even seeking out ? and shops to get a deck optimized.   I am a good deck builder, and have played many Deck building games. I'm not the best player, but I can build a coherent deck by knowing what I need more of, reducing what i don't, and streamlining the process. I don't take a card every time I can, especially if it hurts my strategy.  The current deck variety is a bit stagnant. After over a dozen runs I'm fairly certain I know what strategies work with which characters at this point. I'm hoping they also add more possible End Bosses to the first and second zones, to help make this even better.  Elite bosses are not worth the effort. Most of the time they simply drain your resources or end your run. I literally just plan my routes to avoid them as much as possible. Not good to have a thing in your game I never want to participate in.   Final bosses (stage 3) are also a balance nightmare. I have 17 runs, all losses, and while I have come close, if you get a certain boss, it's better to just to restart than waste your time as the runs can go for hours, especially in multiplayer. It is not a quick, or smooth process to play together as priorty of play doesn't exist. Either it's the entire group of player's turns or it's the enemy. If it's the players, you better be able to discuss your plan, and not take a long time or you will never get through the whole thing. The balance of the game is very problematic, and I suggest you take that into account. I'm beginning to lose interest as I can't seem to beat any of the 3 stage bosses.  Overall it's fun, its not the worst, and in time it could be even better with a few more interesting balance passes.

I'm having so much fun with this game  Multiplayer is excellent, maybe towards the easier side with 3+ players with the insane vuln or doom scaling and multiplayer debuffs, but that's what makes it fun as hell. Multiplayer allows for easy synergies and shreading apart the harder bosses too, while single player gets surprisingly tricky on A9-10. I see a lot of criticism towards the higher ascencions on single player but I personally appreciate it. I dont expect to win every round and it forces me to try strategies and card synergies I dont usually go for. It's a deckbuilder rougelike so it is expected that rng has increasing importance in higher difficulties. What sets this game apart from the first one is how many different viable strategies each character has, Even within those there are opportunities to branch out. Maybe you get an early rare card to build around or a relic that completely changes how your deck functions, You are forced to adapt and make a deck that can counter a variety of enemy types. If you are the kind of player that becomes frustrated when their perfect build gets countered repeatedly, the game can become frustrating at higher ascencions, but I personally appreciate it. I think the devs are going in a good direction by experimenting with mechanics that counter certain types of decks. As fun as infinites are, i enjoy other strategies being viable. Balancing takes trial and error, let's please be nice to the devs <3  People have such different expectations and tastes that it's very difficult to cater to everyone,  I definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys having an easy way to kill off an hour or two of time while listening to a podcast or music. Excellent time killer, just like sts 1 and nothing is forcing you to play higher ascensions if you dont like losing, it is completely valid to enjoy the game at its base difficulties.

Let me premise this by saying that: - I don't like deck builders, so I do not usually play them; - I'm very picky about roguelikes; - I wasn't even going to buy let alone play the game.  That being said, this review is mostly to show support to the devs and balance out the absolute madness that's been going on with the negative reviews.  I like this game. Despite being absolutely terrible at strategies and building my own decks (there is a reason I don't play these kinds of games, oops), StS2 has been a very good experience and a change of pace. The art is gorgeous, the mechanics are clear and simple and you can always make use of a character's unique kit without adding obnoxious amounts of complexity. Ascension levels are balanced to be difficult and give a challenge without actually trying to punish you for wanting higher difficulties. I reached A10, in coop sure, but I did and that's something I've never tried to do but for a few, selected games. That alone is an achievement in my book.  The ability to draw on the map has to be one of the best features for the cooperative games. It's simple, yet it works very well because now if I'm afk I get to come back to the most unhinged doodles on the page and a good laugh.  Not only that, there is A LOT of content to be played, let alone reveal with each Epoch. So really, I only see pros about this.  The game is in early access, but it still feels very polished and less buggy than any 80-bucks AAA game on launch, so this alone should warrant a kinder approach to feedback.  TLDR; the game is worth the full price and the time spent playing it.

My recommendation depends on whether you intend to play at the base difficulty of Ascension 0 or believe the game should typically be played at a higher ascension. If you expect the normal difficulty to be A0, then I would likely recommend Slay the Spire 2.   I believe the highest ascension to be the expected difficulty and in that case the developers have created a frustratingly unbalanced game. A game where even the choices made, such as the nodes chosen can be totally beyond your control. They also continue one of the worst elements of the first game, random events including both a regular enemy encounter or a shop. The game is full of RNG already, it is totally detrimental to force players into base encounters they chose to avoid. When a player avoids a shop because they have little gold only to be forced into a shop is just another lazy punishment.  Another holdover they rely upon for Ascensions is crippling the player to make the game more difficult. This is just an additional lazy choice that doesn't require the developers to introduce any new elements to the game. They just reduce the options at your disposal instead of adding something new to the game.  To start, I do not consider the "Early Access" tag for a game that has been in development for over 5 years. I know they changed the engine for the game part way through, but this isn't an excuse to release a version that there is no way these developers played through on A10 and imagined it was in any way balanced. I truly wonder if they had members of all the teams play through the game and offer any criticism for the difficulties. This is extremely relevant for A9 when every enemy just does more damage and simply chips you down until you end in an unwinnable situation due to the awful RNG.  The reliance on enemies constantly buffing themselves and neutering you is disappointingly lazy. Although it is difficult to desire more interesting mechanics due to the developers inability to create a unique and balanced enemy ability. Bosses such as Vantom introduce a frustrating mechanic from slippery, which is an incredible defense while allowing them to decimate you on certain turns. This is most obvious with a boss such as the Doormaker that they simply removed from the game due to their inability to balance an interesting idea.  Their inability to balance the game is even more odd since there are almost no new aspects to the game. They tweaked 3 of the old characters, but aside from the Defect they do not appear to have any new elements to their character. The Regent is the worst of the new additions mainly due to an entire resource they must produce in order to play certain cards. This is exacerbated when other characters have an event or other opportunity  to add a Regent card to their deck and must consider the fact that they probably can't even produce the Star resource to play one of their cards.  The most disappointing part of the game is the lack of many fundamentally new aspects. Aside from 2 of the 5 characters being new and the rare opportunity to enhance a card (i.e. something Monster Train already introduced in its first game) there is nothing particularly surprising in this sequel. The change from boss relics to the Ancient system is one more awful introduction of RNG. There are 2 Ancients I almost never wish to see, Tezcatara and Vakuu. These two are at best mediocre for 90% of runs and often simply useless. To make Act 2 even worse, Pael is also a coin flip if you are offered anything that truly aids your run. The new mechanic for boss rewards should never end in a deflating experience where you know you will just be limping into your next encounters.

I don't review games still in early access, as if you're buying a game with the understand it isn't finished you've done so to support the creator or because you're impatient. But seeing the flood of negative reviews left by tourists and people unable to comprehend that balance changes will happen has pushed me to at least try to curb the negativity.  This is a good game. If you are picking this game up as your first roguelike deckbuilder then I recommend it- it's forgiving at the early ascensions (difficulties), there's variety with character identity and within each character's card and build selection, and it provides a fun challenge once you've climbed higher. Several friends I have picked it up as their first introduction to the genre and they love it.    If you're returning from STS then I still consider it a better game at its roots (and I have 100'd STS on mobile). That's partially because it's still being balanced- there are cards and relics in the first game so laughably bad you just ignore them, including entire build philosophies that don't function. Each character has more builds they can go through, and the cards overlap easier so you're not tunnel visioned on specific picks. I put a lot of emphasis on variety in roguelikes, and in STS you would often be looking for the same broken combos every run. This game has more variety by far. I'd also say it's a LITTLE easier on average, but that might be because the end boss isn't done (and STS is easy if you're not fighting the heart).  Don't be discouraged by the flux of negative reviews. The game is being balanced, there will be periods it's harder or easier as the dev team works to correct playstyles or enemies that are too strong or weak. The game is in early access, they have a beta branch enabled for playtesting, and things will change.   Good game so far, 8/10, will keep playing.

Once you get to Act 2, the enemies just have double health, constantly gain strength and do massive amounts of damage. Some enemies feel like pocket elites, whereas others just have large health pools. The game essentially treats every enemy from this point like The Champ in Spire 1, who just gains strength each turn until you have to basically block for 30-50 damage or eat dirt. Act 3 just doubles down on this problem, and by this point if you aren't killing enemies in 2-3 turns you're pretty much finished.  .Lack of gameplay variety - The game shoehorns you into certain builds and punishes you for others. Despite the many angles each character has, for some reason you are expected to rely on several metas at once in order to compete. Enemies are built to retaliate to optimised builds rather than giving you an authentic challenge. It feels like they saw players building ridiculous decks and said "well let's just make an enemy to counterract this" instead of actually letting the players do whatever they want and have fun.   .Balances - Why the changes to doom? Why the changes to Doormaker? Why retire cards which fill in the gaps in the playstyle? Why is Knowledge Demon still an annoying boss? Why is Hunter Killer not an elite? I'm tired man. Just scale down the nonsense and let me have fun, please.

The game is in early access and I think most players general expectation is that there will be more contents coming, maybe not week after week but at least there should be a stable stream of content (new cards, mechanics, enemies, maps, even characters?). It's worth noting that adding new content will inevitably change the game dynamic, which could mean a previously weak card can now become a strong pick against certain enemy, or a new card enables more synergy with a pre-existing weak card, making it stronger overall. What I would recommend the devs to do is to really ramp up new contents in their regular updates, and maybe see some of the good ideas generated in the community on card design, mechanics/synergies, even mods that enhances the game visuals (I know there's a Regent special effect mod that's amazing). If players can see new cards unlocked from time to time, and new mechanics / synergies, I'm sure they'll spend more time exporing those options instead of focusing on that 1-2 less damage dealt from their favorite cards.  There's still so many possibilities of this game, please make it to be what it could be. 8/10 I'm starting off by saying that I've played a decent chunk of roguelikes across my time of gaming but haven't played slay the spire 1 so this is more looking over the game as someone who hasn't interacted with this series before now.   Where I'm currently standing, this game is good, all things considered but there are a lot of gripes I've had over my time playing it and I'm writing this to address the problems I've had so far in both singleplayer and multiplayer. I'm currently yet to beat the act 3 boss as I've only gotten through 13 runs that all resulted in a loss but I'm still trying to beat it currently.  - The game tends to have terrible scaling at times for a game so focused on RNG. - The player should lose strength and dexterity debuffs each turn if the enemy gets to as is just makes for unfair combat where the player is constantly punished with debuffs they cannot counteract often and enemies just get to bulk up their damage a bunch if you don't manage to kill them in a few turns. *Possibly adding a card that increases in cost depending on the debuffs you have from 0 cost at no debuffs up to 3 if you have 3+ debuffs, then just remove stacks of it. - Enemies in multiplayer get to hit every player for no logical reason, seeing as players can only hit one enemy per person and the whole point of multiplayer in lots of games it to make it easier so it just doesn't make sense that enemies get over double the health per player plus any buffs they start with. - The damage most enemies get to do is incredibly high 90% of the time and there is very little you can do to stop it unless you are running a specific build. Getting the build you want is tedious because of how much RNG the game relies on for everything. - Enemy health pools are weirdly high so that you can pretty much never win on turn one and therefore must take damage at least once unless you get lucky on your card pulls. - The whole point of roguelikes is to keep trying until you get a really good build but this game just won't let you make a good build as card enchantments can only be applied once per card and cannot overwrite other cards. Even if you make a good build you still rely on the RNG factors that you get the exact cards you need for it when in combat. - Pretty much all the elites are not worth the health loss when the relics they can give are incredibly likely to just be bad and yet they all can do 5-20 damage each turn in just act 1. - Although not applicable to everyone, pretty much every run I've done has resulted in the same enemy pool with the same encounters each run with 1-2 differences every 4 or so runs which I can only assume is terrible luck on the RNG part of the enemy layouts for the map and there is no way that I've found that lets me circumvent this. - The item pool of both relics and potions throughout the game are basically a 60-35-5 split of either being just bad, alright or actually useful which results in most runs feeling really slow and unsatisfying.  I feel like there is potential for the game in future updates but currently the balancing for the game as a whole is driving me away from playing both solo and multiplayer anymore as it feels like I'm just sinking time into it with basically no reward as the unlocks come in incredibly slowly and doesn't feel like it helps me when I end up getting the same loot anyway.

It should go without saying that StS2's art and music are fantastic, so this review is just focused on the gameplay and its balancing.  StS2 has a similar but different design than StS1 and thus requires different play strategies. That may alienate some StS1 players, especially those who were used to building in certain ways in anticipation of certain enemies (prioritizing attacks for Gremlin Nob, needing consistent AoE for Act 2 elites, etc.). I do think that StS2 could use a few more enemies that soft-counter certain deck archetypes, but not [i]hard-counter[/i]. To those who complain about Doormaker: he was rightfully removed off the Beta branch, and I think Aeonglass replaces his role very well as an "anti-infinite" Act 3 boss.  To those who say StS2 is currently too easy: aside from the fact rebalances will continue, do keep in mind that the addition of the alternate Act 2 and Act 3 will add to the difficulty (because you will need to keep your deck more flexible for more kinds of encounters) -- along with the addition of Act 4.  To those who say StS2 is currently too hard: I gotta be completely honest, that's a skill issue. Learn more about the enemies you can encounter and the decks you can make to face them. You're not meant to win every run, but you can certainly win more if you don't always blame the RNG for your mistakes. Current StS1 is DEFINITELY harder (and IMO more luck-dependent, as more of StS1's relics can be duds). Don't give up after just two or three runs.  These are all of my personal design complaints with the current beta: 1. Juzu Bracelet just needs a straight-up redesign. It's low-impact (sometimes [i]negative[/i] impact) and you don't particularly strategize around it even when you get it. 2. Ironclad needs more ways to apply Weak (only 1 card, where every other class has more), either more ways to stack Strength (RIP Spot Weakness, RIP Limit Break) or more payoffs for stacking Strength (RIP Heavy Blade), and maybe one or two more cards that capitalize off of stacking (not just applying, but stacking) lots of Vulnerable. That isn't to say he's currently unplayable; I just think he needs a few more possible synergies. 3. Pael's Eye and Toasty Mittens are a little too specific and niche. IMO both relics could benefit from allowing you to actually choose (to some extent) which cards are exhausted, which would make them more tolerable options more often. 4. IMO Hunter Killer and The Obscura are both just a [i]little[/i] too powerful compared to the other hard pool Act 2 encounters. (But it's better for Mega Crit to listen to the data to determine if that's true.)  I can't think of other complaints. I think the balances between the other relics, between different deck archetypes, between resting or upgrading, between taking events or not, etc. all seem just fine so far. I think it's worth especially pointing out that StS2, more-so than StS1, allows larger decks to perform well when built carefully, and removing Strikes and Defends is not as critically necessary to win (if, again, you have the right cards/relics to accent them).

It's a constant "play around this niche (but interesting) mechanic while the enemies have MASSIVE HP pools and hurl huge numbers at you while often negating all of your damage" My problem is the game feels balanced for singleplayer and the solution for multiplayer balancing is just doubling everything's HP, but that doesn't work in practice especially when even in singleplayer, the enemies tend to be meatbags. Like how do I shield for 20+ dmg every turn and still pump out enough damage to kill the thing beating on me before it scales to an even more unattainably ridiculous power level? I guess the complaint just comes down to certain fights feel impossible without good RNG and that doesn't feel good to play into at all. I love the game at its core, but this needs fixed desperately.  Overall, I'd say if the balance issues get fixed this is without a doubt something I'd recommend to anyone. With the balance issues though....ehh, bring a thinking cap, some determination, and a can-do attitude (maybe a few buddies and a couple of beers too) and you'll get to the top eventually. Before the second major update you had some level of influence over the card rewards you get, I could get the deck I wanted with every class pretty consistently. And that's what made this game fun. That's what separated slay the spire from all the other deck building games out there (other than being a great game and we'll balanced). But now even that isn't the case anymore. I understand the desire to make a game difficult and I'm all for it. But this is way too much. The recent changes to certain enemies were way over the top and unjustifiable in my opinion. The flying Doritos change made him a run ender. If your deck relies on spells, you can hit that give up button the moment you see him. Every turn for every spell you play he gets 3 attack, and of course he multi attacks every 3rd turn. The door maker was replaced by the eonglass boss. So if you meet him and your deck is not exhaust warrior, status defect or minion reagent, you can go ahead and hit alt F4 on your keyboard because most likely you're not going to survive 35 dmg first turn with immunity for 4 turn and of course every 6 cards you play you get a status card that deals dmg to you at the end of your turn. It's such a frustrating game. The core gameplay loop is awesome and highly addictive but it is a 25 dollar DLC that just copy pasted 60% of the original game. And that's a perfect encapsulation of the baffling design choices. Why just remake part of the first game and add two new characters and a handful of new content? Why not include everything from the original if that's how you're going to design it? Why make some of the regular encounters harder than elite encounters? Why have no consideration at all to balancing encounters? Why have a large percent chance to have encounters in ? rooms? Why don't ? mark room triggers activate when there are encounters in them? Why are draws seeded rather than randomized? Why is there so little synergy in most runs if they are seeded and not randomized? Why is it so common to not draw any useful cards during major rounds? Why does the Vantom have 9 Slippery!? It does 45 damage in 3 turns and you have to attack it 9 times before you even start damaging it? Most runs will allow maybe 4 cards per turn on average and you need to block 45 points of damage and attack 9 times before you even start ticking away at the 170HP it has? So with 12 cards you need to literally waste 9 of them and then with 3 remaining cards you need to block 45 damage? 60% of all characters starting HP? When in most cases you can get maybe 15 block from a card on average? And with the aforementioned often not drawing any block cards when you are attacked for 27 damage? As an Act 1 boss? And that's really not even one of the more poorly designed enemies. With the right character and run it's completely trivial. It just brings into question basic game design questions. What challenge am I supposed to be overcoming in this encounter? With Vantom at least there is an answer to that question: Have a ton of free damage cards that you can burn him down quickly and just enough block to survive. There's really only one answer which is why it never feels challenging; it's either trivial if you meet the challenge or impossible if you don't. But at least it has an answer. Many of the encounters don't. The enemies in them hit hard, and have high health, and can negate damage, and limit your block, and start out strong, and ramp, and do sustained damage, and do burst damage, and limit your ability to draw and play cards. So am I supposed to focus damage? block? status? balance? single target? spread out damage? speed? longevity? No. You are either supposed to have a God tier run or just take so much damage that your run is effectively over. You might as well just have a number flash on the screen that tells you how much damage you took in the room. I get that there is always going to be randomness but I would like a bit of strategy in there as well. It could just be so amazing and instead it feels like a mobile game.
